# Notifications and Observability {#sec-notifications-observability}

```{python}
#| include: false
import pointblank as pb
pb.config(report_incl_footer=False)
```

A validation only helps if someone finds out about the results. When a check fails on a scheduled
run at three in the morning, a report saved to a folder does not help anyone. When validation runs
unattended, a person or a system needs to be told when something goes wrong. This
chapter covers sending results out of the validation process, whether as a message in a chat
channel, as metrics in a monitoring system, or as a custom alert for whatever tools you already use.

These notifications are sent through the actions from @sec-thresholds-actions, so you already know
when they run. A step action runs when an individual check reaches a threshold, which suits an
urgent alert about one check. A final action runs once after the whole plan and sees the complete
results, which suits a summary of the run. Pointblank includes two ready-made notifiers, one for
Slack and one for OpenTelemetry, and you can write your own for anything else. We use
`game_revenue` for the examples that run.

```{python}
game_revenue = pb.load_dataset(dataset="game_revenue", tbl_type="polars")
```

The most common place to send notifications is a chat channel, so we start with Slack.

## Slack notifications

The `send_slack_notification()` function creates an action that posts to a Slack channel through an
incoming webhook. Before you connect it to a plan, it helps to see what the messages will look like.
If you call it with `debug=True` and no webhook, it prints sample messages instead of sending
anything, so you can check them without a real channel.

```{python}
pb.send_slack_notification(debug=True)
```

The preview shows the two kinds of messages the notifier sends. The step message describes a single
failing check, with its type, severity level, step number, column, and time. The summary message
describes the whole run, with the highest severity, the number of steps, and how many steps failed.
The values here are made-up samples, such as `column_name` for the column. Both messages use default
templates, and you can replace either one. The `summary_msg=` and `step_msg=` arguments take
template strings with placeholders in braces, which are filled in when the message is sent. Here is
a custom summary template.

```{python}
pb.send_slack_notification(
    debug=True,
    summary_msg="Validation of {tbl_name}: {highest_severity} ({n_failing_steps} of {n_steps} steps failed)",
)
```

The summary preview now reads "Validation of example_table: critical (2 of 5 steps failed)", using
the same sample values. The step message is unchanged, since we only replaced the summary template.
Step templates can use placeholders such as `{step}`, `{column}`, `{type}`, `{level}`, `{value}`,
`{autobrief}`, and `{failure_text}`. Summary templates can use `{tbl_name}`, `{highest_severity}`,
`{n_steps}`, `{n_failing_steps}`, the per-level counts like `{n_critical_steps}`, and a few more,
such as `{tbl_row_count}` and `{validation_duration}`. A custom step template works the same way.

```{python}
pb.send_slack_notification(
    debug=True,
    step_msg="[{level}] step {step}: {type} failed on {column}",
)
```

The step preview now reads "[critical] step 1: col_vals_gt failed on column_name". Using
`debug=True` like this is a quick way to get both templates right, which is much easier than
adjusting them after they are connected to a real channel.

To send real messages, you give the function a webhook URL, and it returns a function that you
attach as an action. The same notifier works in both roles. It sends a step message when used as a
step action and a summary message when used as a final action.

```{python}
#| eval: false
notify = pb.send_slack_notification(
    webhook_url="https://hooks.slack.com/services/XXX/YYY/ZZZ"
)

validation = (
    pb.Validate(
        data=game_revenue,
        thresholds=pb.Thresholds(critical=0.10),
        actions=pb.Actions(critical=notify),
        final_actions=pb.FinalActions(notify),
    )
    .col_vals_not_null(columns="player_id")
    .interrogate()
)
```

As a critical step action, the notifier posts an alert as soon as any check reaches the critical
threshold. As a final action, it posts a summary at the end of every run. This example is not run
here, because it would post to a real channel.

Where you attach a notifier matters as much as what its messages say. A step action runs once for
each step that reaches its threshold, not once per failing row, so a check on a million rows still
sends only one alert. But attaching a notifier at the warning level across a large plan can still
produce a flood of messages on a routine run, and people soon learn to ignore a channel like that.
A better setup is to use step notifications only for the critical level, where an immediate alert
is justified, and to let a single final action send the summary. That way the channel gets one
summary per run plus the occasional urgent alert.

## Exporting to OpenTelemetry

Chat messages are for people. For monitoring systems, the `emit_otel()` function exports validation
results as OpenTelemetry signals, so they end up in whatever observability platform you already use.
Used as a final action, it can send metrics, traces, and log records about the run.

::: {.callout-note}
## Requires the OpenTelemetry SDK and a collector
The examples in this section are not run here, because `emit_otel()` needs the `opentelemetry`
libraries installed and a collector or backend set up to receive the signals. To run them, install
the SDK alongside Pointblank and configure it to send to your collector.
:::

```{python}
#| eval: false
otel = pb.emit_otel(enable_metrics=True, enable_tracing=True)

validation = (
    pb.Validate(
        data=game_revenue,
        tbl_name="game_revenue",
        final_actions=pb.FinalActions(otel),
    )
    .col_vals_not_null(columns="player_id")
    .col_vals_lt(columns="session_duration", value=40)
    .interrogate()
)
```

Metrics are on by default (`enable_metrics=True` is written out here for clarity). They include
counts of steps and test units passed and failed, the pass rate, step durations, and how many steps
reached each threshold level, all named with a `pb.validation` prefix that you can change with
`metric_prefix=`. With `enable_tracing=True`, the run is recorded as a trace with a span for the
whole validation and a child span for each step. The `enable_logging=True` option also sends log
records for steps that reach a threshold, starting at the level set by `log_level=` (the default is
`"warning"`). The `extra_attributes=` argument adds your own labels to every signal, such as an
environment or a pipeline name, which makes the data easier to filter once it reaches your
monitoring system. The data engineering scenario in @sec-playbook-data-engineering shows this kind
of setup in a larger pipeline.

## Building your own notifier

Slack and OpenTelemetry are the two built-in notifiers, but you can send results anywhere with a
final action of your own. Inside the action, `get_validation_summary()` returns a dictionary
describing the run, and you use its values to decide what to send and where. To start, this action
just prints a few of the summary's keys so we can see what it contains.

```{python}
def show_summary():
    s = pb.get_validation_summary()
    print({k: s[k] for k in [
        "tbl_name", "highest_severity", "n_steps",
        "n_failing_steps", "n_critical_steps", "overall_health_score",
    ]})

_ = (
    pb.Validate(
        data=game_revenue,
        tbl_name="game_revenue",
        thresholds=pb.Thresholds(warning=0.02, error=0.05, critical=0.10),
        final_actions=pb.FinalActions(show_summary),
    )
    .col_vals_lt(columns="session_duration", value=40)
    .col_vals_in_set(columns="acquisition", set=["organic", "google"])
    .interrogate()
)
```

Both steps failed, and one of them (the acquisition check) reached critical, so `highest_severity`
is `"critical"`. The overall health score from @sec-quality-scoring is 83.8, pulled down mostly by
the 574 rows that fail the acquisition check. The full summary has more than this, including counts
of steps at each level, lists of passing and failing step numbers, the dimension scores, the table's
size, and how long the run took. Once you know what is in the summary, you can make the action
decide what to do based on `highest_severity`.

```{python}
def notify_on_severity():
    s = pb.get_validation_summary()
    if s["highest_severity"] == "critical":
        print(f"PAGE: critical data quality failure in {s['tbl_name']} "
              f"({s['n_failing_steps']} of {s['n_steps']} steps failed)")
    elif s["highest_severity"] in ("error", "warning"):
        print(f"LOG: {s['highest_severity']} in {s['tbl_name']}")
    else:
        print(f"OK: {s['tbl_name']} passed all checks")

_ = (
    pb.Validate(
        data=game_revenue,
        tbl_name="game_revenue",
        thresholds=pb.Thresholds(warning=0.02, error=0.05, critical=0.10),
        final_actions=pb.FinalActions(notify_on_severity),
    )
    .col_vals_lt(columns="session_duration", value=40)
    .col_vals_in_set(columns="acquisition", set=["organic", "google"])
    .interrogate()
)
```

The action runs at the end of the interrogation. Since the acquisition check reached critical, it
takes the first branch and prints the "PAGE" message. In a real notifier, the `print()` calls would
be replaced with a call to an email service, a webhook, or a ticketing system, but the structure is
the same: read the summary, check the severity, and send the message. This works for any
destination that does not have a built-in notifier.
